metadata.title: The CRA Ladder.
metadata.subtitle: Concrete–Representational–Abstract, One Lesson
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Plain register: does differentiating fraction addition for three levels mean three separate lessons? It doesn't — the CRA ladder runs Concrete, Representational, and Abstract as three entry points into the SAME lesson, all converging on 1/3 + 1/2 = 5/6. Lands the carry-out that Claude builds one shared target with three rungs, tested by whether every rung reaches the abstract result without skipping a step.

beats.narration_text: A teacher first types: three levels, run it separate. Not quite — the real question is whether one lesson can run as three entry points. Here's how the CRA ladder does that.

beats.narration_text: One third plus one half. Three rungs on one ladder. Concrete: fraction circles — push a one-third piece and a one-half piece together and watch five sixths appear. Representational: a tape diagram split into thirds and halves, finding the shared unit before the arithmetic. Abstract: the equation itself — one third plus one half equals two sixths plus three sixths equals five sixths. A student below grade level starts at Concrete. A student at grade level starts at Representational. A student above starts at Abstract. Every rung climbs toward the same result.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR — three rungs, one ladder, 1/3 + 1/2 = 5/6

beats.narration_text: The design move is the arrows between rungs, not the rungs themselves. Three journeys run at once, all aimed at the same abstract destination. A student who reaches five sixths with the circles is ready for the tape diagram. A student who can draw the diagram is ready for the equation. The rungs aren't separate tracks — they're one shared staircase, with three places to start climbing.

There's a catch called the expertise-reversal effect. The concrete support that helps a beginner — the physical fraction pieces — becomes noise for a student who already holds the representational picture in mind. The support that was scaffolding turns into clutter. So the CRA ladder isn't a fixed setting for a student — it's a path, and the rung that helped yesterday may not help today.

production_viz.label: THE RUNG THAT HELPED YESTERDAY
production_viz.caption: the rung that helped yesterday is noise today

beats.narration_text: Scaffolding carries a three-part contract: contingency — support matched to where the learner is right now; fading — steady withdrawal as skill grows; and transfer — the learner ends up doing it alone. Skip fading, and support that once matched five sixths on the circles just stays in place forever. Removing a rung and checking whether the learning still holds is how you find out if it was scaffolding or a permanent prop.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — the contract behind the ladder

production_viz.label: THE SCAFFOLDING CONTRACT
production_viz.caption: skip fading, and five sixths never lets go of the circles

beats.narration_text: Claude doesn't build three separate lessons — it builds one shared target with three rungs to reach it, and the test is whether every rung gets there without skipping a step.
